nameStory: The sanderling gets its name from Old English 'sand-yrðling,' meaning 'sand-ploughman' — a perfect description of how these busy little birds work the sandy beaches like tiny farmers tilling the surf line. Watch them scurry along the water's edge, and you'll see exactly why our ancestors thought they looked like miniature plowmen turning over the sand for treasure.
description: Sanderlings are small, energetic shorebirds about the size of a robin that you'll see racing back and forth along sandy beaches like wind-up toys. They have a distinctive thick, straight bill and stocky build that sets them apart from other small sandpipers. These arctic nesters are long-distance travelers, showing up on New England beaches during spring and fall migration, and some stick around through winter along our coast.

idTips.label: Bicycling Run
idTips.description: Watch for their unique running style along the surf line — they move with a characteristic 'bicycling' motion of their legs, running in quick bursts then stopping abruptly to probe the sand

idTips.label: Missing Back Toe
idTips.description: Unlike other small sandpipers, sanderlings completely lack a hind toe, leaving only three toes pointing forward — if you get close enough to see their feet in the sand

idTips.label: Thick Bill
idTips.description: Their bill is noticeably thick and blunt compared to other small sandpipers, looking almost stubby when seen in profile

idTips.label: White Wing Stripe
idTips.description: In flight, look for a bold white stripe running along each wing that flashes prominently as they wheel over the waves

idTips.label: Beach Preference
idTips.description: They strongly prefer sandy beaches over mudflats or rocky shores, staying right at the water's edge where waves wash up

idTips.label: Flock Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen in tight flocks that move as one unit, creating a mesmerizing wave-like motion as dozens of birds run in sync along the beach

habitat: Look for sanderlings on sandy ocean beaches throughout New England, especially wide, flat beaches where they can run along the surf line. They prefer the wet sand zone right where waves wash up and rarely venture onto mudflats, rocky shores, or inland areas. Popular spots include Cape Cod's outer beaches, New Hampshire's Seacoast, and Maine's sandy stretches like Old Orchard Beach.

seasonality.spring: Spring migrants pass through from late April through May, often showing patches of rusty breeding plumage mixed with their pale winter colors. They may pause to feed heavily on beaches before continuing to Arctic breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Most sanderlings are on their Arctic nesting grounds, but a few non-breeding birds may linger on New England beaches through the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Peak migration occurs from July through October, with adults arriving first in late summer followed by juveniles. Fall birds show crisp gray and white plumage.
seasonality.winter: Some sanderlings overwinter along New England's coast, particularly on Cape Cod and the Islands, appearing pale gray above and bright white below in their winter plumage.

funFact: Sanderlings are among the most extreme northern breeding birds on Earth, nesting only on the coldest Arctic tundra where July temperatures barely reach 41°F — yet these same tiny birds will fly all the way to South America for winter, making them true world travelers covering both poles!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small sandpipers like Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers, but sanderlings are the 'beach runners' — if you see small sandpipers doing that distinctive bicycling run along sandy surf (not mudflats), they're almost certainly sanderlings. Memory trick: 'Sandy sanderlings stay on sand, not mud.'
contextualKnowledge: Some scientists have suggested sanderlings are so different from other sandpipers (especially lacking that hind toe) that they deserve their own separate genus called Crocethia, but most experts now agree they're similar enough to other small sandpipers to stay in the genus Calidris with their relatives.
compareHints: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper. They're also the beach specialists — while Least Sandpipers prefer muddy areas and Semipalmateds use both habitats, sanderlings stick almost exclusively to sandy shores and have that unique missing hind toe.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
